subtopic: TEMPORARY COMMISSION ON KOREA-ACTION OF CANADIAN DELEGATE

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): I am now in a position to supplement the information I gave on March 10 regarding recent developments in the work of the united nations temporary commission on Korea and the position taken by the Canadian representative, Doctor Patterson.
We have now received a full report from Doctor Patterson on what happened. It appears that as the March 1 anniversary of the 1919 declaration of Korean independence drew near there developed a strong undercurrent of demand among the Korean people for some announcement concerning their future to be made on that date. Accordingly members of the united nations commission then in Seoul discussed and agreed among themselves, and cleared by telephone with the commission chairman, Mr. Menon, then m New York, that the acting chairman, Mr. Liu, should make a public statement on March 1, saying that the commission would accept the advice of the interim committee to observe elections in south Korea. General Hodge proclaimed the date of elections for May 9 after Mr. Liu had made this public statement. Doctor Patterson, who was in Tokyo at the time, was not consulted, although he had left his telephone number with the principal secretary of the commission on his departure from Seoul, with the request that he be called should any important matter arise; nor was a regular commission meeting called in order to discuss the matter. Accordingly, at the next regular meeting of the commission Doctor Patterson, under instructions, drew attention to the irregularity of the procedure by which this important decision was reached. He pointed out that if the commission were to proceed in this manner its impartiality and authority as a properly constituted united nations commission would be undermined. As a result of this intervention the commission re-examined the whole position very carefully in several days of private discussions and at the end decided that there should be a formal vote to record the position taken by each member.
On March 12 the commission formally decided "to observe elections announced by

United Nations Commission on Korea
the commanding general of the American forces to be held on May 9, 1948, provided that it has ascertained that the elections will be held in a free atmosphere where democratic rights of freedom of speech, press and assembly will be recognized and respected". The vote in favour of this resolution was 4 to 2, with Canada and Australia against, and Syria and France abstaining. In voting on this resolution the commission in effect recognized the validity of Doctor Patterson's objections to the irregularity of the earlier informal agreement to observe elections. I think that the importance which the Canadian representatives on the interim committee of the general assembly and the united nations temporary commission on Korea have attached to united nations bodies observing proper constitutional procedures has made a valuable contribution to the work of the united nations.
The reports in the press that Doctor Patterson had walked out of the commission were incorrect and misleading, both to the Korean people and to persons abroad. When the commission decided to observe elections in that part of Korea accessible to it, Doctor Patterson cabled us for further instructions. Pending the receipt of these instructions Doctor Patterson, as was only right and proper, informed his colleagues on the commission that he would not be able to take an active part in the work of the commission until he had received further instructions from Ottawa. He has continued to attend the meetings of the commission, nevertheless.
Doctor Patterson has presented the views of the government on the commission faithfully and well under difficult circumstances. His experience and knowledge of the Far East have enabled him to give us sound and helpful reports on the background of developments in Korea.
The government has decided that it will not be necessary to recall Doctor Patterson for consultation, because he has been able to send us a very full account of what happened. Instructions have been sent to Doctor Patterson authorizing him to continue to serve with the commission, because the commission conceives its duties to be to observe, consult and advise Koreans and the United States military government authorities regarding the conduct of these elections; but the responsibility for running the elections rests with the United States military government authorities and any action towards the establishment of a government in Korea following the elections will not be on the strength of the resolution
of the general assembly but on the legal position of the occupying military authorities. Further, the chairman of the Korean commission has drawn attention to the fact that the commission has the authority to withdraw at any time if it is not satisfied that it can perform a useful function in remaining in Korea to observe the manner in which the elections are to be held.

subtopic: TEMPORARY COMMISSION ON KOREA-ACTION OF CANADIAN DELEGATE
speechtext:
Do I take it from the minister's statement that the elections will be held under the auspices of the United States occupying forces rather than under any organ of the united nations? Is that the point?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The proclamation fixing the date for the elections and the legal basis on which the elections are being held are the acts of the military authorities and not as we first understood, namely, that an attempt would be made to have it appear that they were being held under authority derived from the resolution of the general assembly which provided for an election for the whole of Korea and not for only one part thereof.

speechtext:
I desire to lay on the table two documents. The first is entitled "Private and Public Investment in Canada, Outlook 1948", and the second deals with "Production of Basic and Building Materials in Canada, Outlook 1948". They were prepared by the economic research branch of my department. The French text of these two papers will be available as soon as the translation and printing are completed.
The first paper is a forecast of the likely volume of investment based on returns from some 13,000 business establishments and institutions and information supplied by governments, federal, provincial and municipal. The outstanding feature of the report is the fact that it indicates for 1948 a capital program of $2-8 billion, the highest in Canada's history. If realized, this will be about 17 per cent in excess of the S2-4 billion spent in 1947, although somewhat less than 5 per cent more in volume. The program involves an anticipated $1-6 billion on new construction and SI * 2 billion on new machinery and equipment, representing increases of 21 and 12 per cent respectively over 1947 levels.
The second paper, based on production plans of Canadian business, indicates that output of
Senate Bills

eight out of nine basic materials is expected to be maintained during 1948 at the high levels achieved in last year, while in the ninth, coal, an increase in volume of 15 per cent is anticipated. Production of thirty types of building materials show further improvements for 1948, with increases of over 20 per cent indicated for bathtubs, steel pipe and fittings, gypsum plaster, gypsum lathe, rock wool batts and construction tile. Smaller increases are expected for all other items except for two, where decreases are anticipated.

The application of these, in so far as eleetrotherapeutie equipment is concerned, was postponed nearly seven years to January 1, 1948, owing to a shortage of supply of material and equipment. The question of a further postponement has now undoubtedly been raised by reason of action in the United States where a five-year period of grace has been given. It will be noted that the similar period of grace in Canada has been seven years. There is an outstanding difference, however, in the interference caused by this equipment in the two countries. In the United States a large part of transmitting equipment is very high powered and is not affected to as great an extent as in Canada, where the greater part is of a much lower power.
Interference by the operation of this equipment is a serious matter in radio communications in Canada unless adequate means are employed to control the radiation. Safety radio services, such as aids to air and marine navigation, police and fire department radio, are frequently blotted out by radiation from diathermy machines at distances of hundreds of miles. A further period of grace in this matter of suppressing this type of interference would delay the proper development of these and other high frequency services.
While it is proposed therefore to enforce the regulations effective January 1, 1948, I would point out that the inspectors of the radio branch of the Department of Transport have done nothing to disrupt existing operations where interference is not being
encountered. However, where interference is found, operators of this type of equipment will be required to install the necessary shielding if the equipment is to continue to be operated.

Has the report the minister has just made anything to do with the difference in cycles between Ontario and other parts of Canada? The minister shakes his head. I should like to know whether he says yes or no.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply

With regard to members of the medical fraternity in small towns who are operating eleetrotherapeutie machines which are causing radio interference, will the minister give them time to replace the machines which are banned by this order? Each member state shall make such arrangements as suit its particular conditions for the purpose of associating its principal bodies interested In educational, scientific and cultural matters with the work of the organization, preferably by the formation of a national commission broadly representative of the government and such bodies.

Why are toilet articles costing more than twenty-five cents taken out of the schedule?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the other way round; toilet articles costing more than twenty-five cents are left in and are subject to tax. The exclusion was for this reason. It was found that the imposition of the tax on lower priced articles, particularly brushes and combs, created a completely distorted price range. It threw the thing out of line. The manufacturers and distributors of that type of article convinced me and my officials that the tax would create a completely distorted price picture. What we were attempting to get at was the higher priced fancy articles sold as gifts.

The minister's explanation seems hardly consistent. He objects to putting a 25 per cent tax on an article that sells for twenty-five cents, yet he put a tax of 40 per cent on something that sold for a nickel.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Soft drinks?
Right.

The minister says that this tax was imposed for a number of reasons, and I should like to repeat the reasons he has given. First, he says the tax was not put on for taxation revenue primarily, but if there were some tax revenue, that would be welcome. Secondly, in an article in New Liberty a while ago he said that this tax, along with other taxes, was to plug a leak, the leak being, I suppose, the United States funds disappearing from our hands. Next he said it was to induce 
people to postpone buying; in other words to restrict buying. At another time he said it was to discourage imports from the United States, and finally he said it was to withdraw purchasing power.
Turning now to toilet articles which cost more than 25 cents, dresser ware, and so forth, the minister knows there has grown up in this country over a period of forty years a plastics industry. Some firms do nothing but manufacture and sell plastics, marketing them not only in Canada but in South Africa, India and other parts of the world. For the life of me I cannot see how any one of the explanations for this tax given by the minister in any way helps our economy, whereas the tax most certainly bludgeons this particular industry out of existence. The industry uses probably only eleven per cent of United States content. Most of its component parts are obtained in Canada. That was not so a few years ago, but it is so now. The chemicals, bristles, and so forth, that go into the manufacture of these articles are made in Canada. I ask the minister if eleven per cent of United States content is of sufficient importance to murder this industry which has been functioning in Canada for forty years. The minister has already learned from one or two of these firms how serious the situation is.
On the other hand, under the exchange conservation bill, the Minister of Trade and Commerce has the say as to what goods may be imported and what United States content they may have, and his idea may be entirely different from that of the finance minister Surely trade and commerce is the lifeblood of this country. I suggest to the minister that this is not the proper way of handling our business.
One more thing. The minister suggested that this was a temporary measure. I suppose therefore it was drawn up in a hurry. Yet the fact of the matter is that the very day after the tax was announced on the evening of November 17, the tax officials throughout the country were on November 18 making inspections and visitations in respect of this tax. That is what I call snooping; it is the gestapo method. I would like the minister to explain why these things go on when business is the lifeblood of our country.
To come back to my question, does the minister think that a United States content of eleven per cent is of sufficient importance to justify his putting this industry out of business?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I gave a good deal of consideration to the brush industry, and I do not believe that the imposition of this tax is

Excise Tax Act Amendment
going to put them out of business by any means. Their volume will probably be reduced. I would hope that it will be reduced, because that is the purpose of the tax, but from the information I have, it is not going to ruin the business, as my hon. friend has suggested. It is true that eleven per cent is not particularly high; still it is an appreciable United States content. There is this other point, that we are trying to effect not too drastic but a certain reduction in consumption in Canada all along the line, particularly of less essential articles. One cannot reduce the consumption of food and essential clothing, but if we are to continue to play our part and export partly on credit we must create again what we had up to a little over a year ago, a surplus of production over consumption.
Mr. TIMMINS'. What difference does it make whether the toilet articles are made out of plastics or ebony or some other wood? Surely one particular group should not be singled out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Rightly or wrongly the toilet articles group has been singled out since 1933 for this type of tax. In wartime that was considerably expanded and that continues. Personally I look forward to the day when we can get rid of this type of tax. It is not the type of tax that I personally like to keep permanently in the tax structure. I would prefer a simpler structure but under conditions like the present, when we are attempting to use the fiscal weapon as a means of restricting consumption this is a line in which it can be legitimately employed.
As I understand, toothbrushes have been taken out completely.

What is the difference between toothbrushes and hairbrushes so far as one's ordinary personal necessities are concerned? Why should toothbrushes go free and not hairbrushes? speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

One facetious answer might be, I suppose, that a good many more people have teeth than hair. At any rate, toothbrushes were eliminated in the first place because they are in the low-price bracket.
They are a real necessity, and therefore they were eliminated at the very outset. I am serious about this because, after all, when one comes to an industry which is at the point of life and death, the matter is quite serious. It is more serious than the minister makes out, whether the industry should or should not be taxed when it does not come within any of the five categories which the minister has set out from time to time as comprising the things which should be taxed for the purpose of saving United States dollars. other parts of the world. We ought to give serious consideration to taking goods of this kind out of the purview of the act. I repeat, our own industry comes first and when it ceases to do so we have made a mockery of ourselves in this sort of legislation.

The other day, replying to a question, the Minister of Finance said that the reason certain household articles such as refrigerators were taxable while similar articles for industrial or business use were not-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Industrial or commercial production.
Those which enter into production or the making of one's living, I understand, are in general exempt. I understood that to be the answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not necessarily in all cases. That is the general principle followed.

It is a principle that might be extended to other articles. There are two items mentioned here, firearms and outboard motors, which in a large number of cases in the northern parts of Canada are used in the production of goods or as a means of making a living. There are occupations such as trapping, prospecting, fishing and so on in connection with which these articles are purchased, and they are bought not as luxuries or for sporting purposes but for the purpose of enabling the purchaser to make a living. In such cases would the minister consider exempting them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We gave careful consideration to those two items, because in northern Canada the outboard motor is a part of the trapper's equipment, and the same applies to a lesser degree to firearms. However, we came to the conclusion that it would not be practicable to do that because the tax is put on at the wholesale level. Those two articles go out through jobbers, as do others, and administratively it would have been almost impossible to handle them. One would have had to have individual applications and it would not have been possible. On balance we came to the conclusion that the outboard motor, even when used for that purpose, would have to be subject to the tax.

If that applies to these two items, does it not also apply to the articles mentioned in the previous paragraph, that is to say gas refrigerators? If the tax applies at the wholesale level or the manufacturer's level in the cases that have been referred to, I suggest that it applies in the 
same way all the way through. I do not see how you apply that in one case and not in another.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that that type of refrigerator is a clearly identifiable type of product made for trade purposes and not for household use.

Administratively it would not be impossible. It might be slightly inconvenient but when you consider the inconvenience to which the public is put at the present time, I suggest that the government should share a little of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The matter was given careful consideration and it was felt not to be practicable. The reasoning my hon. friend puts forward would apply with force to the low-priced automobile, which is used in a great many cases by doctors and others for professional purposes.

Going further down the list we find certain photographic supplies, slides, films, projectors and so on designed for industrial or professional photographer's use. There is another example where that type of equipment may be necessary for a person to make his livelihood and there is a possibility of creating a distinction between that which goes into professional use or industrial use and that which may be bought for sporting purposes. Sporting cameras and the cameras used by the public generally are different from those used by photographers in their trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: One of the principal reasons in this case for including these items is the fact that they have an exceedingly high import content, and we are anxious to discourage such imports as much as possible; and yet you cannot put under licence or quota the import of that sort of thing. It was not felt practicable to do it.

A small industry in Port Elgin known as Keystone, but which we consider one of our large industries, will be hit heavily by this measure. Will the minister keep in mind the fact that a great number of people depend on that industry in Port Elgin for their livelihood? At various times there is talk in the house about decentralization. Here is an excellent- opportunity

Excise Tax Act Amendment
to practise decentralization in concrete form, by keeping such an industry as this functioning.
Its products consist mostly of brushes. I called it a small industry but I am probably wrong, because at one time it was recognized as one of the largest industries in the British commonwealth of nations. I understand that briefs have been presented to the minister which describe the situation better than I am able to do. This company manufactures low-priced as well as high-priced articles. Would it not be wise for the minister to consider raising the ante and getting it up a little higher? If you go out and buy a shaving brush, you do not get it in the 25 cent list. You might get for a dollar a shaving brush that would give you some satisfaction. The list of articles covered by this 25 per cent excise tax is such that it will hit the chap in the lower income brackets. If we could raise the ante a little it wmuld not hit him as heavily. Another thing I should1 like to point out is that all the articles this concern produces are essential for health purposes. Once more I would ask the minister to consider raising the ante up from 25 cents to whatever he thinks would be worthy of consideration.

I want to follow up what was said by the hon. member for Dauphin regarding outboard motors. These should be free of excise tax to those who will use them for professional purposes, such as guides, trappers and resort hotel owners. I am especially interested in this matter because of the fact that in my riding the outboard motors for the whole of Canada are made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Very fine motors too.
Yes, they are fine motors.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The tax on clocks and watches, of course, is not proposed under this resolution.

No. I mentioned that it does not come under this resolution; but it is hindering export trade the same as this tax is hindering the export trade of outboard motors today and will continue to do so. I am afraid that it will also have an adverse effect on labour. In fact it has had that effect already; lay-offs have taken place in these various firms. Consideration should be given to the suggestion of the hon. member for Dauphin that guides, resort owners and others who want outboard motors for professional use should be given them without taxes. All these motors are sold with a guarantee, the same as electrical appliances are sold. Every dealer has the name of the purchaser, and it would be a simple matter to have the dealer return the tax to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
None whatever. It is
strictly on current account.

purpose of restricting the purchase of many of the durable kinds of consumer goods which are either imported or contain a significant import
content.
The minister made it quite clear that this was temporary. The immediate effect of his saying that it was temporary was that, the next day and the day after, people who had given orders for dresserware immediately returned their goods to the manufacturer or wrote to the manufacturer cancelling their orders. That happened to a great number of people in the brush industry' and in the dresser-ware industry'. Still the measure is temporary. What is happening now is this. These goods have probably a seasonal sale. Orders are taken during the year and some time in the fall delivery is made. This year orders are not being placed. In other words it may be the minister's wish that there shall not be any sale of these goods, that there shall not be any manufacturing of these goods, and that there shall not be any money made in this industry but that some other industry shall get the benefit of that business. The fact of the matter is that because the minister says this is of a temporary nature this industry is stifled. I would like the minister to tell the house just how temporary this measure is and, further, just what is the explanation of the words "significant import content." Does that mean five per cent, ten per cent or what?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As to the time question, Mr. Chairman, I cannot assume the role of a prophet in this matter. This phase of our dollar conservation program will be gotten rid of just as quickly as we can, consistent with the restoration of our reserves to what we believe is a safe level. As to the use of the word "significant", I have already' dealt with the various reasons which prompted the use of this fiscal weapon. The United States content was one of those reasons. Perhaps I did not stress some of the others as much as I should have in my radio speech, but on several occasions during the course of this debate in committee I have emphasized the necessity of reducing the consumption even of articles which had almost no United States content.
Then may I stop the minister there for a moment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Others may hold that this is wrong.
What would be the benefit to Canada of putting a tax on an article which had almost no United States content?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I must repeat that one of the objects of this program is to reduce

the over-all Canadian consumption of all articles to a point where we are again producing more than we are consuming. We were in that position in 1946, when total Canadian production was two or three hundred million dollars in excess of what we were consuming and importing. In 1947 we caught right up with it, however, and consumed and imported just about what we produced. In other words, in order to continue to export four or five hundred million dollars worth of goods abroad we had to live on our fat; we had to dig into our reserves. Now our reserves have reached the point where we cannot do that, and we have to create again an over-all current account surplus if we are to continue to export on credit.
But can we afford to dissipate what we have in the way of production in order to bring about this over-all picture the minister speaks of?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not a question of dissipating what we have in the way of production. What we must do is consume a little less ourselves in order that we may lend it or give dt to others who need it. The United States is in the fortunate position of having a large over-all current account surplus which enables it to export substantial quantities of goods to other countries on credit. We had that surplus up to the end of 1946. We do not have it now, and that is because our people are using up domestic consumption and imported articles at a rate which just about balances our total production. We do not want to slow down very much, but we have to pull in our belts just a little bit and, as I have said before, live within our own means and within the means of our customers.
Then will the minister consider dropping this excise tax before he drops the conservation measure?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it would be very' improper for me to say which of these measures we should take off first. For what it may be worth, though, I can indicate that I would think this is one of the measures I would want to get rid of first.

I am sure the minister would not want to carry his austerity program to such a point that he would have us stop buying brushes necessary for personal hygiene. Would he consider raising the price ranges so the tax would apply only to brushes costing more than a certain figure? This would permit people in the lower income brackets to continue to buy these brushes.

Excise Tax Act Amendment
If the minister would not consider this point would he tell us his reasons for not considering it?

I want to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Bruce. This has been the subject of a very great deal of criticism on the part of the man who wants to buy an article selling for perhaps SI or $1.25. They indicate that prices have gone up to a certain extent as it is, and when you add this tax you add very materially to the cost of standard articles which I think the minister will agree are necessities rather than the luxury items he is trying to suggest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Hon. members will realize that, I have had exactly the same representations they have received, and from the same sources. I listened to them as sympathetically as I could and went into the matter very carefully. I came to the conclusion that this tax should continue; that it was not going to ruin these particular types of business, as has been suggested. I came to the conclusion that in the very low ranges, this five, ten and fifteen cent stuff, it was quite improper that there should be any tax because it was impracticable. But it must be remembered that there has always been a tax on these articles when sold in sets, and now the tax is simply being extended to the articles when they are sold individually as brush, comb and mirror. For years these articles have been taxed when sold in sets.

I believe the government should still give consideration to this excise tax. It depends entirely upon whose business is being ruined, upon whose ox is being gored, as the old saying goes, as to whether or not the tax seems reasonable. I was interested to see the minister and the government switch over from the argument that this excise tax was put on because if this were not done it would give an advantage to our own manufacturers as against our former sources of supply, namely across the border. Apparently that did not take any too well with the Canadian public, so the minister developed the argument, I think somewhat late in the debate, that it was necessary for the Canadian people to tighten their belts in order to restore the over-all surplus position which we had some j'ears ago but which we lost last year.
I cannot believe, Mr. Chairman, that the government is serious, that it is sincere, that it is not endeavouring really to fool the members of this committee when it says the excise tax is placed on this very limited number of
articles for the sole reason of causing Canadian consumption to decrease.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I never said that was the sole purpose. It is one of several purposes.

If the government is sincere about limiting purchases by our Canadian people -and I do not think it is as necessary as the minister makes it-then there certainly are means which are a hundred times more effective than the specious argument he brings forward to justify this excise tax.

I take it that as soon as this measure is passed this whole thing is crystallized and nothing more can be done. After all, many of the appliances included in these four clauses are now the normal

At the request of the hon. member for Quebec South, who was organizer of the Liberal party in 1935 in Quebec, I made a list of the taxation imposed by Bennett each year, and it was used as propaganda during the election. Now we have more taxation. I do not put the blame upon the minister. He is a likeable chap, but he suffers from the bad companionship of those wizards in the Department of Finance. Let us get rid of them. Who in this committee will say I am wrong when I denounce them?

Let me repeat what I said about the deputy minister of finance-and I am extremely glad he is not here today. He used to come here to adorn the House of Commons by his presence; but he is not here today, and it is a good thing he is not. He should not be in the department, either. Why? Let us get rid of these people. Let us get rid of Clark. Let us get rid of Towers. Let us get rid of Rasminsky. Let us get rid of Donald Gordon. Let us get rid of all these fake wizards, and then we shall have sensible taxation and the people of this country will be able to carry on without too much difficulty.
I am sorry to have been obliged to say this, but I suffered much when I thought of it and when I thought of the poor people who are suffering because of the stupidity of these so-called wizards who would not be tolerated as advisers in any other government. I am fed up with them.

That is what he has been informed. That is the situation today. I think that letter is based upon the real facts which exist in this country. People with average incomes are finding it difficult to purchase some of t'he essentials of life for members of their families,'especially when there are young children. A refrigerator is an essential article. It is necessary to preserve food and there is nothing luxurious about it. It is one of the most essential articles required by families in the low and average income groups. Why the government should undertake to impose such a tax at this time on people in the low-income group is certainly more than I or any of these people on low incomes can understand. The government are distinctly wrong, and if the amendment should fail to carry I appeal to the minister and the government as strongly as I can to exempt refrigerators from this tax.

I wish to say a word about this tax on refrigerators. The minister told us that one of the purposes of this tax was to curtail consumption. It was suggested by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario and the hon. member for Moose Jaw that production and consumption could have been curtailed by rationing United States dollars to these manufacturers just as was done with the automobile industry. The minister replied to the effect that there was a lot of domestic material content in these refrigerators, such as copper
Excise Tax Act Amendment

and steel, which would be available for export if not used in the manufacture of refrigerators. But the refrigerator manufacturers in Canada, I would point out, have established the Canadian content over a period of years and drawbacks are provided for exports, so that the department knows exactly how much of United States content there would be in each model of refrigerator the manufacturer makes. Furthermore, the manufacturer would not use any more copper or steel, because what they import from the United States is the heart, which consists of the compressor and thermostatic expansion valve. You cannot build a refrigerator without these component parts, and that is what they are bringing in from the United States. So that if dollars were rationed on the basis of past imports they could build only as many refrigerators as they bring in component parts for.
Another thing about curtailing consumption is that you are curtailing consumption of the wrong people. The rich people are not concerned about paying $25 or $38 more for a refrigerator if they want one. They buy the more expensive models, ten or eleven cubic feet, and they cannot get them now. What this tax is doing is penalizing the veterans and the young couples who are starting up housekeeping and need a refrigerator. This tax makes them pay 25 per cent more for it. The minister said: They will save their money in the meantime and buy a refrigerator when the tax comes off. But they cannot save their money, because they have to have that refrigerator this summer. Many veterans' homes have no cellars and many ice companies will not take on any more customers. There was a shortage of ice last year and, no doubt, will be again this year, because the natural ice went out before the ice companies had finished their cut. I do not believe the tax will do anything to curtail the consumption of the rich people, but it does hit the veteran and the newly married couple. Furthermore, it puts members on both sides of the house, particularly on the government side, in an embarrassing position.
I hope the government will not get the support of its members for this tax, but, if it does, what will that member say to the veteran whom he is taxing 25 per cent more on his refrigerator? The veteran will be getting literature from his branch of the legion showing that his member voted for this tax.
If we vote for this tax we are breaking our pledge to the boys who went overseas and fought overseas. It is like saying to them: You were over there fighting for us and we gave you a nice brochure saying for $13.42 
a month you get all this and a nice sum of money when these goods were tax-free; but now you are through school, have a wartime house perhaps, the war is over, and you can pay the tax just like anybody else, and so the veteran is hooked for the 25 per cent tax that he should not be asked to pay. For these reasons I am supporting the amendment.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just
before the committee rose at six o'clock the Minister of Finance had raised a point of order with respect to the amendment which I had moved a little earlier. I may remind the committee that my amendment was a very simple one. It merely asked that clauses 1, 2, 3 and 4 of what is now perforce regarded as one resolution be deleted. The Minister of Finance, as I say, raised a point of order with respect to this amendment. I intend to answer the argument put forth by the Minister of Finance on his own ground, namely, by quoting from May and other authorities; but before I do so, may I point out to the committee and to you yourself, sir, the utterly impossible position in which the government is putting this house by the course now being pursued by the Minister of Finance.
This afternoon we took the position that we had before us six separate resolutions. On the basis of that position we contended that we had the right to vote on those six separate resolutions as six separate propositions; in other words, that we had the right to accept some and reject others. The minister argued against that position, after resolution No. 1 had been defeated on a free vote, and contended that what we had was not six separate resolutions but just one resolution. I immediately did what seemed to be the only course left to us, by moving the amendment now before the committee.
The minister now contends that my amendment to delete the clauses we object to is out of order. In other words, it is a case of the government saying that the opposition simply cannot have an opportunity to vote on these individual propositions either one way or the other.
I contend that the government has a pretty serious responsibility resting on it by following this course and by raising points of order of this kind. I felt, however, from the attitude of the Minister of Finance, and from things I thought I heard him say, although he did not rise from his seat to say them when I moved my amendment, that he was satisfied with this procedure. It seemed to me he felt that here was a chance to vote on the question whether or not we accept or reject the first four parts of his resolution. We are told now that we cannot have that opportunity, that we have either to take as a whole or to reject as a whole these six different propositions.
I submit that such a procedure is entirely contrary to the spirit of the citation which I read this afternoon from Bourinot, and which is in the other authorities as well, namely, that it is always proper to ask for a division of a complicated question into its distinctive and constituent parts. Therefore I am sorry, in the name of parliamentary democracy, that the minister has taken this position, in view of the place in which it puts the opposition in this free parliament.
But, Mr. Chairman, the minister has chosen to cite from page 544 of May, thirteenth edition, reading part of the paragraph, and contending, on the basis of a part of that paragraph, that my amendment is out of order. The part he read from page 544 was as follows:
Proposals for the variation or modification of taxation can therefore be made in the committee; but these proposals must be grafted upon the financial scheme submitted by the government, and must not affect the balance of ways and means voted for (the service of the year.
I forget whether he read the rest of the paragraph or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I went right on.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Fine; I shall do the same. However, after that I wish to come back and point out the part he failed to read. It goes on:
Amendments, therefore, can be proposed to substitute another tax, of equivalent amount, for that proposed by the government, as, for instance, a proposal to substitute probate and legacy duty on real property as an alternative for an inhabited house duty; the necessity of new taxation to that extent, being already declared on behalf of the crown.
Now I point out that in that same paragraph there is this first sentence which the minister neglected to read:
Though it is the function of the committee of ways and means to impose rather than to repeal taxes, examples of the repeal of taxation effected in this committee are to be found upon the journals.
There is a footnote at the bottom of the page, which gives a list of a number of cases where the repeal of taxes has been effected in the committee of the whole.
Now, Mr. Chairman, and this is the crucial part of my argument, it seems to me that the feature about the citation which the minister quoted and which has not been noted is this. The paragraph as a whole is dealing with two separate things. In the first sentence it deals with the right to repeal certain taxes, the right to get rid of certain taxes altogether. That is a very brief sentence without any provisory qualification added to it. In the second place this paragraph deals, not with repealing or
Excise Tax Act Amendment

wiping out a tax altogether, but with varying or modifying a tax that has been proposed by the government; and the part of the paragraph which the minister read says that when you try to do that, and only when you try to do that, you must stay within the general framework of the government's balance of ways and means. The paragraph goes on to give the reason why the committee must do that. This must be done so as to carry out the general instruction that any money measure must in the first instance have had the recommendation of the crown.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that that citation which the minister read, and which has often been brought out in this house as a reason why the opposition cannot move any amendment in committee of ways and means, has been completely misinterpreted. It is not a citation which says that no changes can be made in committee of ways and means. It simply says that if you are trying to vary or modify a tax proposal, you must stay within the general framework of the government's proposal. Again I say that paragraph deals with two things. It deals with what you must do if you are seeking to vary or modify a government tax proposal, but it also permits the complete repeal of a tax proposed by the government, and to this permission no proviso is attached. The Minister of Finance read from only one page in May, thirteenth edition. May I ask him to turn to certain other pages. I ask him to turn to page 560 of the same volume, which reads:
Proposals to reduce a burthen upon the people may be made in the house or in committee, no special form of procedure being prescribed for such a motion . . .
The paragraph goes on to say that this may also be done in connection with the introduction of bills which are strictly confined to the reduction of a tax or charge upon the people. Then the paragraph continues:
It follows that amendments for the reduction of such charges, as taxes, rates, salaries, tolls and penalties, can be moved when a bill is considered upon report-
Perhaps I had better go on. I referred to the minister's not reading the whole of a paragraph. This -had better be put on the record too. The paragraph continues:
-and this has been permitted even when, by indirect effect, an amendment created a certain amount of charge. For instance, it was held allowable, upon this stage, to strike out an exemption from a tax, which had been agreed to by the committee on the bill; and also to omit a clause imposing a charge upon the ratepayers, although the omission of the clause left other parties, already liable by law, still chargeable with certain expenses.

So in that paragraph on page 560, the tone of which is clearly set out in the first sentence, that it is always competent for a committee to reduce a burden upon the people, is a specific list of things which it is possible to repeal; taxes, rates, salaries, tolls and penalties. What we are seeking to do in this amendment is not to vary or modify a tax, as is set out in the citation quoted by the Minister of Finance. We are seeking to get rid of one altogether. If hon. members will turn again to page 519 of May, thirteenth edition, pages 518 and 519, they will find this interesting paragraph. This .paragraph follows a section that has dealt with the necessity of having the royal recommendation in connection with any bill that will involve the expenditure of money or the imposition of a burden. Note this paragraph:
It follows, as a matter of course,-
And this is fundamental to British parliamentary practice having to do with the imposition of taxes.
*-that a motion to alleviate the burthens upon the people is not within the scope of the standing orders relating to the imposition of charges upon the people.
In other words, a motion to alleviate a burden is not governed by the standing orders that have to do with expenditures and taxes, which require the royal recommendation. The paragraph continues:
A bill for diminishing or repealing a tax or other public burthen, unless the imposition of a new tax is proposed by way of substitution, is introduced without the royal recommendation or preliminary committee stage.
That again is very clear. I pick up now another book, and this time it is Bourinot, fourth edition, in which there is a long, list of things that can and cannot be done in committee of the whole with respect to taxes. Finally, at the end of the paragraph that appears on pages 431 and 432 there is this clear-cut sentence:
A proposition for the repeal of a duty is in order, and cases will be found where a proposed duty has been struck out in committee.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that that citation fits exactly the terms of my amendment. My amendment is a proposition to strike out in committee a proposed duty. I have left that one to the last because it is so clear; but actually in terms of the theory of parliamentary procedure I feel that the citations I have quoted from May are more to the point, and I hope that they will have cleared up this confusion about the citation which the Minister of Finance read. Clearly that citation would apply if my amendment were an

Excise Tax Act Amendment
attempt to modify or vary a tax imposed by the government. If I were seeking to do that, I would either have to show that I had the governor general's approval, or I would have to show that it was within the framework of the government's balance of ways and means. But that is not what I am seeking to do. I am not trying to modify or vary a tax at all. I am asking this committee to exercise the fundamental right that has adhered to parliament down through the ages, and that is to relieve a burden placed upon the people. I am asking that certain items of taxation be struck out altogether, and I submit that my amendment is clearly in order.

That is one thing that can be done. Changes can be made within the framework of the scheme that has been approved by the crown.
It is also competent for any member to propose another scheme of taxation for ithe same purpose, as a substitute for the government plan. But it is not regular to propose a new and distinct tax, which is not a mere increase or diminution of a duty upon an article already recommended by the government for taxation, though it is the function of this committee to impose rather than to repeal taxes.
Then comes the last sentence; and the reason I have read the whole paragraph is to get it clearly in the mind of the committee that this rule sets out several different propositions.
A proposition for the repeal of a duty is in order, and cases will be found where a proposed duty has been struck out in committee.
My whole argument turns on this, Mr Chairman, that there are at least two different things set out by these rules which it is competent for the committee of the whole to do. One is to make variations or modifications. When the committee tries to do that it has to follow the proviso or qualification the minister has quoted. The other is to strike out a tax altogether; and when the committee seeks to strike out a tax, neither in May nor in Bourinot is there any such proviso or qualification as that quoted by the minister. The minister is trying to take a qualification that applies to one procedure and attach it
Excise Tax Act Amendment

to another. I submit that not only is that an invalid way of arguing, but that we have had a little too much of it in this house.

I enjoy very much listening to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre; - that is why I did not rise earlier to call him to order. The situation is obvious. When the resolution was before the committee, Mr. Chairman, you decided that it should be considered paragraph by paragraph. Then an appeal was taken to the Chair. The ruling of the Chair was that the resolution should be taken as a whole, and that ruling has been supported by a majority of the house. It is a defiance of the ruling of the Chair. Mr. Speaker gave his ruling and declared that the resolution should be considered as a whole, not according to its several parts. That ruling was given support by a majority of the house. Then, after all that, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre tries to educate us as to what should have been done. It is done. It is like arguing about spilled milk. It is finished. How can he come before you and ask that you act in the opposite way to the decision of the Chair? I cannot conceive it. For me the thing is as clear as crystal water. There is no doubt about it; and when the hon. gentleman thinks the matter over he will realize that. What has Bourinot to do with it? What has May to do with it?

I mean the Speaker's ruling.

Evidently the hon. member was not in the house when the vote took place ; otherwise with his usual acuteness he would have known what happened. The chairman gave a ruling; the Minister of Finance appealed

that ruling, and my hon. friends on the government side voted against sustaining the chairman's ruling. Consequently we now have what the Minister of Finance wanted; we have one motion instead of six, and that motion is amendable.
Now that the whole resolution is back before the Chair-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
There is a point of order before the Chair and I should like to give my ruling now, because I do not think there is any point in further discussing it. At the outset of his speech the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred to the minister as wanting certain things, but I should like to remind him that the house itself decided that this should1 be submitted as one resolution. In regard to the other points the hon. gentleman raised, I think I should read Beauchesne, third edition, page 182, citation 500:
Though it is the function of the committee of ways and means to impose rather than to repeal taxes, examples of the repeal of taxation effected in this committee are to be found upon the journals.
And I should like hon. members to notice this:
Proposals for the variation or modification of taxation can therefore be made in the committee; but these proposals must be grafted upon the financial scheme submitted by the government, and must not affect ihe balance of ways and means voted for the service of the year. Amendments, therefore, can be proposed to substitute another tax, of equivalent amount, for that proposed by the government, as, for instance, a proposal to substitute probate and legacy duty on real property as an alternative for an inhabited house duty, the necessity of new taxation, to that extent, being already declared on behalf of the crown.
I followed the hon. member very closely. In his amendment he certainly does not propose any way of raising any tax of any sort. In view of citation 500 to which I have referred, I rule that the point of order raised by the minister is a proper one, and that the amendment is out of order.

It seems to me that what is suggested here is nothing more or less than what is done every day when we are dealing with estimates. The amendment offered by the hon. member is not a substitution of another tax. It is not a suggestion of any increase. In fact, according to the minister, this is not a tax.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order; the ruling is not debatable. I have listened to the arguments for and against.
