Mr. Chairman, since the resolution has not yet carried, and since it is all before the committee, there are one or two observations I should like to make. My first remarks will be about paragraph (b) of section 1, and then I shall speak about section 2. I would refer, first, to electrical items, and then to motorcars.
A few days ago there was a discussion in the house as to how the Minister of Finance could return excise taxes once they had been paid in. Today I received a letter from the Canadian Association of Radio and Appliance Dealers, which might be of some assistance to the minister in connection with the returning of the tax, if later on it were decided to have that done.
This letter is addressed to myself and reads thus:
We notice in the press that the 25 per cent excise tax on electrical appliances is being discussed in the house and, particularly, the feasibility of returning the tax moneys already collected to the consumers.
The Canadian Association of Radio and Appliance Dealers has discussed this matter with many of its members and with other branches of the electrical industry, and we stand ready to assist the government in carrying out a reversal of the procedure by which this tax was collected.
I might say that this association is using good judgment in offering to assist the government. The letter continues:
For example, for guarantee purposes our members are forced to record the name and address of each electric refrigerator purchaser (they have a five-year guarantee). Therefore, there would be no problem in having cheques mailed to each of these purchasers for the amount of the tax. In addition, this association is prepared to go further and by national coverage in the press invite consumers to apply to their retailer for the rebate.
This association stands ready to facilitate the removal of this tax which in the eyes of the young couples and veterans who enter our stores seems to be an unnecessary burden.
I thought perhaps the minister would like to have this letter on Hansard. If he decides 5849-158J
to return the tax later on, then he will know this association is ready to assist his department.
I agree with all that has been said by hon. members on this side of the house, although I am not so sure about those on the other side. I have no doubt there are just as many hon. members on the other side who would like to speak about the tax on radios and electrical appliances. But of course party followers just cannot do that.
Might we have a little bit of order over there? It is not fair to the hon. member who is speaking.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.
I know how hard it is to keep from talking. However it does not bother me at all; I can go ahead and say what I have to say.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I would ask hon. members to refrain from talking when an hon. member is trying to make himself heard.

I had just said that I aixf sure there are as many members on the government side as there are on this side who would like: to comment about these taxes. I am sure the minister has had many conferences with his followers; but it is difficult for a government supporter to speak as freely as we on this side can speak. We are not tied down as are members on the government side of the house. I was on that side myself for five years, and it used to irk me to sit over there and say nothing, and not be invited to say anything.
I had just said that I agree with what has been said on this side of the house about the tax on refrigerators and other electrical appliances. It is going to be a great burden.
I should like to ask if the minister surveyed other ways in which he could have conserved all the money he required to conserve. I have in my mind just one item; and I believe I may make reference to it without being out of order. Last year we imported coal to a value of almost S150 million, and paid United States railroads about $75,000,000 to haul that coal to our border. That, made a total of $225 million in United States money we could have conserved if we could have purchased that coal in Canada. I am not going to say we could have purchased all of it, but certainly we-could have purchased a large part of it.
I have often wondered why ministers of finance-and I am not asking only the present one-have not been able to tell us why they are not allowed to arrange things so. that
Excise Tax Act Amendment

Canadians can use their own products. Had we used our coal, we would have saved a great amount of these iniquitous taxes. Perhaps that is not the right word to use; but they are iniquitous so far as the people who have to pay them are concerned. And it would have saved the minister a good deal of trouble in these troublesome times.
Then, may I say that motorcars are no longer luxuries to workingmen. For years governments have been encouraging working men to live outside the cities and to buy perhaps five acres or one acre of land. These workers have been encouraged to live within ten or fifteen miles of the cities, and thousands of them have accepted that suggestion. In those days there was no trouble about securing motorcars.
Look at the position they are in today. When I go home a multitude of workingmen come to see me and ask me how in the world they can buy new cars. Their cars are worn out, and they cannot pay the 25 per cent excise tax. They ask me what they are going to do, and state that they have been put out of the cities and they do not know how they will get to the cities to do their work.
The same applies to rural schoolteachers who live in towns throughout Ontario and drive out to the rural schools from those towns. I had one come to see me when I was home on the last occasion. He was wondering how he was going to buy a car, in view of the 25 per cent tax.
The same applies to the ordinary clergyman who has two or three field charges. I have had communications from them asking how they are going to buy cars and pay the extra 25 per cent tax. So I say that no longer can a motorcar be considered a luxury to anyone who has to make a living. Certainly they are not luxuries to the. workingmen. They use motorcars because of necessity. I do not know whether it is too late to have the minister change his mind, but I for one believe that something should be done to help the ordinary man. I am not speaking about the rich man because he will buy a motorcar, no matter what it costs. I know many people have bought new cars at exorbitant prices and jx 25 per cent tax means nothing to them. But to the ordinary everyday worker who perhaps lias to go into the city to carry on his job or, if he lives in the city, has to go from one lend to the other, a motorcar is not a luxury; it is an absolute necessity.
I have not taken much of the time of the committee when I could have taken up a lot. What is the use? These taxes are all in operation, but the amount of correspondence

I have received and the number of people who have come to see me made me feel that I should speak. Having given this information to the government, I feel that I have done my duty and cannot do anything more.

I hesitated to take part in this debate until I had an opportunity of listening to the accumulated wisdom of the members of the various oppositions and also the explanations that the minister has given. I feel that it is easy for an opposition to oppose a tax. In opposing this measure I do not want to be put in the position where I am opposing a tax because it is a tax and I know it will be unpopular with the people. I have supported many tax measures which the government has brought into this house and which I assume were quite unpopular. However I feel that this tax is in a particular category as far as unpopularity is concerned.
I am not going into the constitutional argument that has been advanced to the committee, because there are plenty of lawyers to take up that phase of the matter. However it does appear to me that the minister's explanation of the way in which this tax was brought in was unworthy of the brilliant talents which it is acknowledged the minister has. When the C.C.F. moved to throw out all the taxes it appeared to me to be a gesture that anyone in opposition could well afford to take. But I do not think the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre does justice to his responsibility as a member.
Despite what the hon. member for Davenport has just said about the necessity of a workman having a motorcar, I feel that the present taxes on motorcars are not particularly onerous. Anyone who can afford to pay $1,700 or $1,800 for a new car can afford to pay an additional $130. That payment will not make it impossible for him to carry on his job. I am quite sure we all feel that the government is justified in trying to keep out of the country these high-priced cars that, as a matter of fact, some of our hon. friends drive.
Hon. members in this house know the minister very well and I think we all have a great deal of confidence in him. I do not think the public of Canada have had the same opportunity to know him. With the constitutional crisis that has occurred in the democratic world as we know it, I am afraid that the public might be a little concerned about this departure from regular parliamentary practice in the introduction of these excise tax proposals.

Excise Tax Act Amendment
Perhaps I may be forgiven for offering a word of advice. It seems to me that we in the house would have been glad to accept the minister's explanation of the urgent necessity that prompted him to bring in these taxes. If he had come before us and said, "I realize that this was an unconstitutional way of doing this and I regret the urgent necessity that made it necessary for me to bring them in"; I think if he had thrown himself on the generosity of the house all members would have been glad to give him a hand in support of his proposals.
I come now to the actual items of taxation. I know the minister is opposed to dirt just as much as he is opposed to sin. I think vacuum cleaners could well be left off and refrigerators also. If the minister made one or two minor concessions of that kind I am sure they would represent only a small reduction in revenue. I think if he came before us and proposed a 50 per cent excise tax on some of these items we would probably be glad to support him. Some of these things are definitely luxuries.
He put a 25 per cent impost at the manufacturers' level, but a 50 per cent tax at the same level would be just equal to the present luxury tax at the retail level on jewelry and that sort of thing. There are many things which would be more of a luxury than the wedding ring which many men have to buy. Those of you who are married know that is a necessary item, and yet we have been willing to pay a 25 per cent tax at the retail level. As I said, I think the tax on motorcars is all right. I was in Windsor the other day and thej' assured me that they had enough orders to keep them going for the next two years. I do not feel that this tax will be very harmful as far as that is concerned.
In closing, there is just one thing I want to say and this is not advice to the minister, it is advice to the government. The government is very conscious of the fact that they will be fighting two by-elections in British Columbia within the next couple of months. As I said last time I spoke, we are particularly sensitive about the fact that we have no cabinet representation. It has been pretty well assumed in Canada that at long last British Columbia, for the first time since confederation, is to have the ministry of fisheries.
The hon. member for New Westminster.

The present incumbent of that position is a close personal friend of mine, a man of great personal charm. However I feel that his particular talents could
be used by the government to better advantage in some other ministry, and I think he would be the first one to concede that point. I suggest that if the minister is going to put over these excise tax proposals with the voters of British Columbia, the best thing to do would be to have the Prime Minister appoint the hon. member for New Westminster as Minister of Fisheries. It would be one of the most popular moves the government has ever made, and I am quite sure the people of British Columbia would show their appreciation at the polls.

Mr. Chairman, we have heard quite a lot about this resolution. We are getting near the time when we hope to adjourn for a space and no doubt there is much to be said for letting this go, though still unconvincing to the minds of many hon. members on both sides of the house. But the more I hear about it, the more it seems to me that the evils and difficulties attendant on it are set forth, and the less there is that satisfies me that it should be passed.
For a few minutes tonight I am going to look back and trace briefly the history of this resolution. Let us see what was originally stated to be the purpose, and let us see if that, purpose seems to have been changed a great deal in mid-career. Finally, and much more important, let us see whether there is any likelihood of its achieving the purpose for which it was originally put forward, or indeed any other purpose.
I should like to turn back to what the Minister of Finance said in his broadcast in the middle of November last. After dealing with the embargo measure which we have already passed as Bill No. 3, he went on to say:
Import restrictions alone will not be enough to keep down our use of goods which contain a high proportion of parts or materials from the United States.
I pause there a moment to point out that apparently there has been a very considerable change so far as that is concerned, because we now have goods on this list which have only a trifling proportion of United States parts. He went on:
Many of these goods are produced on a large scale in Canada and we cannot properly limit and ration the imported parts and materials.
Incidentally no explanation has ever been given to my satisfaction why that is so. Incidentally, again, may I say it seems to me there is a considerable argument for using Bill
Excise Tax Act Amendment

No. 3, which is now law, instead of this jumble of provisions which seems to begin nowhere and to end nowhere. He continued:
I am therefore proposing to use the same fiscal devices as we used during the war to restrict purchases of this type of goods.
I want to read a little more, and I ask the members particularly to notice what I shall read now to see whether it does not appear that there has been a considerable departure in outlook from the intention then set forth. I am not criticizing that. I am only saying it would look as if the bill is very different from what was in the mind of the Minister of Finance at that time. He went on:
The government will ask parliament to place an excise tax of 25 per cent on a wide range of these durable consumer goods, the purchase of which-
Note this:
-can normally be postponed by the average family if necessary and most of which are of a less essential character.
Listening to the debate this afternoon, it didi not seem to me that many of the taxes come within that class at all. He went on:
This tax will apply to sporting goods, outboard motors, pleasure launches, firearms, oil burners, motor cycles, musical instruments, cameras, radios, phonographs and to most types of electrical home appliances.
That is what the minister said in November last. I now come to what he said in December last, and I read briefly from his speech on December 16. First of all I want to read this extract, in which, speaking of the special excise taxes, he says:
Their first and primary purpose is to discourage the sort of expenditure which adds to our imports from the United States.
I want to emphasize that. This was a measure originally put forward for the saving of United States exchange. It is unfortunate that the minister has had difficulty in getting the figures. We have not yet got them, but I do not believe it will be a very bad guess to say that those figures will show a very trifling saving in United States exchange. I say that for this reason. The minister felt at the outset that no figures at all could be got; but when I persisted, perhaps somew'hat unduly, he was good enough to say he would get the figures. I must not say too much by way of anticipation; but I do not believe I would be wrong if I said that the minister will prove right to this extent, that when those figures are produced they will be of the nature which he himself prophesied, that they will not show any substantial saving so far. If they do not, it will not be surprising because, after all, bear

in mind that the only direct saving of United States exchange has to come through a lessening of consumption of goods made in Canada which have United States components. There is precious little evidence yet of much falling off in the consumption of Canadian goods. Moreover we know that many of these goods have only a trifling amount of United States parts in them, some much less than ten per cent, some an even more trivial percentage. So I think we shall find that there is no evidence yet of any substantial saving in United States exchange.
I pass on to the minister's second reason, and always bear in mind that this reason was put forward in November and again in December as a measure for saving United States exchange. But evidently he felt that that would not be a sufficient reason, and there were several others. I now come to the second reason, and I think this is a complicated and difficult one. It seems to me to have two or three parts inconsistent with each other. I will read very briefly:
A second reason for these taxes was to limit so far as practicable the degree of discrimination against regular suppliers in the United States and their dealer organizations in Canada.
In other words, as under Bill No. 3, a great many goods were to be excluded from Canada either wholly or largely, because, as the minister says, it was felt desirable to ease the situation for those United States exporters who would be cut off from this market. That may be a laudable objective; but along with that the minister goes on to point out, and this is one of the means of arriving at his objective, that we must also prevent Canadian manufacturers of these goods from deriving too much benefit from the fact that United States goods are kept out of the market. That perhaps has something to be said for it; but the means taken are, I suggest, rather odd, and bear in mind that this has precious little to do except indirectly with United States exchange. The means taken is to put on this tax. The minister says this tax is put on so that Canadian manufacturers who otherwise, according to him, would have jacked up their prices by reason of the absence of United States goods will not be able to do so, or at any rate so that the first 25 per cent of such a rise in price will be by way of this tax which the government will get, and therefore the minister suggests that Canadian manufacturers will be prevented from deriving this very unfair profit. I hope myself that Canadian manufacturers would have done nothing of the kind. There is nothing to suggest that competition might

Excise Tax Act Amendment
not have kept the prices down. In any event, the point I wish to make is this. In order to reach this questionable and quite illusory benefit, who is made to suffer? The Canadian taxpayer because he has this 25 per cent tax put on him.
Again let me point out where we are in the matter of having United States exchange. We have come to the point where the minister, in order to do what he deems to be fair to United States exporters who are shut out of our markets, puts on this tax.
Another point arises there which I think it is desirable to remember, and this leaves me so much unconvinced about this whole measure. As soon as you press the minister as to any one of his reasons, he immediately flits off to another reason, and the reason the minister has to do that is, I suggest, that this whole measure is a confused jumble. I said a moment ago it starts nowhere and ends nowhere. It is a hodgepodge of inconsistent and sometimes conflicting reasons.
The minister also brings the tax argument in here. If the price is going to go up, let us get it by way of tax, he says. I want to point out that this measure comes right back on the taxpayers and on a class of taxpayers who are very ill able to bear it. The minister I think recognizes that. I have no doubt that he is receiving very strong appeals from taxpayers, and that brings me to another argument.
The minister says: Oh, but we have to have an over-all surplus in Canada if we are to export goods abroad, and therefore we have to cut down consumption in Canada. Well, that may also be a very proper objective, but what I object to about this measure is this: Why does he select the people who are paying this tax to be the only people who are to be affected in this way? If we are to cut down consumption in Canada, why not do so in a very much more general manner? There is no justification whatever that I can see for dealing with the matter in this way.
We now come to the minister's fourth reason, and that is taxation. The minister finds himself in some difficulty because, on the one hand, he does not want us to regard this as a taxation measure, but on the other hand he suggests that the taxation will not be unacceptable after all; and in answer to the people who say that he has a huge surplus, he points out quite properly-I wish he would do so oftener-"Oh, yes, we have a large surplus this year, but we have been making large advances to overseas countries, as I have already indicated; and, on a cash basis, including those outlays, our income is only moderately in excess of our outlay." In other words, we have, first of all, the argument about saving United States exchange, which I believe will prove to be trivial in the extreme and utterly unwarranted. We have that as a reason for this measure-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Nevertheless we have balanced outgo and income.
You have been given such wide powers that you will be able to do it all. Isn't that the idea?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: You are complaining about what you demanded last summer that we should do.
I am only complaining about the way you did it. You will see what happens now.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: We have done it. That is the important thing.

I have referred to the combined provision for protecting the United States manufacturer from the effect of what will be done to him by the Minister of Trade and Commerce; the Minister of Finance apparently feels sorry for what the Minister of Trade and Commerce will do to the United States manufacturer, and so he takes a whack at the Canadian manufacturer. But as a matter of fact, the person at whom he is finally really taking the whack is the Canadian taxpayer, and that is what I think is so unwise and unwarranted in this bill.
Put it this way. Why put a 25 per cent tax on this small group of people who happen to be affected by these taxes, rather than a much smaller tax, if the minister feels it necessary, on the whole of the larger group? The minister said, and I rather respected him for saying it, that probably he had not gone far enough, that probably the austerity measures had not gone far enough. Well, we can all agree that the mess they got us into by the decision of June, 1946, is a serious one. We can all agree that drastic steps have to be taken.
There is a fifth argument the minister used. That fifth argument was that, while these prices were going up and while the tax would have to be added to what the people would pay, still it was useful as a deflationary measure, because it would1 help to mop up extra purchasing power which existed and in that way help to bring a cure. I see the minister's point there, but I feel that the people who are being subjected to this tax, if it were explained1 to them that they were being made the sacrifice in order to help to cure the mistakes of the administration in expanding our means of payment far beyond
Excise Tax Act Amendment

what they should be expanded-if the people who are paying this tax were told that, I think they would be greatly surprised' indeed.
I submit that this measure has been changed in various ways from the position in which it stood1 at the beginning. The minister has told us frankly that many changes had to be made, because they found that great distress was being caused in certain quarters, and those changes had been embodied in an amendment. It is quite true that has been done, and in the course of it certain other changes have been made which the minister has found it hard to explain. As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Fraser Valley took him on the other evening by reason of the fact that there are certain articles on which the tax is left when used for domestic purposes but on which it is not paid if those articles are used in a business.
That shows how this thing has to be chopped and changed so that the original basis has in many ways disappeared, and therefore we can doubt very much whether the minister is satisfied with it, or whether even he believes it is likely to do what it sets out to do.
Therefore, even at this late date, having regard to the evident fact that the government is quite uncertain as to what is wise or unwise in this; having regard incidentally to what the minister told us today, that they are still so uncertain as to whether the tax is imposed on the right people that they will retain in the bill the power to relieve certain other categories; having regard to all that, it seems to me it is very proper, even at this stage, for us to ask the minister to reconsider the whole situation.
We have a measure which it is stated is devised to save United States exchange. When you argue on that basis they go off on to several other bases. When the United States exchange argument will not hold good we have an argument about cutting down expenditures, which I have tried to indicate is wrongly dealt with in this bill. If the government are going to cut down expenditures, do not select merely this group of taxpayers, but do it in a more general way. And, so far as the United States exchange is concerned, let us remember that the government stubbornly refuse to take one of the remedies which we have advocated and which we think they will have to take one day, and that is to deal with the Canadian dollar and its value in a realistic manner. That would help the United States exchange situation.
For all these reasons, I still hope the government will see fit to withdraw a measure which is so unpopular, and, what is more important, so unwise.

I rise tonight to explain my vote as I did a year ago in connection with the veterans affairs, and I sincerely hope I shall not have to explain my vote in connection with veterans affairs this year, because, if I have to explain it, it will not be satisfactory to the government.
In this connection, I spoke against the tax on frigidaires the other day. I spoke against taxation on what I call the poor man's automobile. I still think the Minister of Finance is wrong, and I still think he should take advice from some members of his own party in particular and, if not from them, at any rate from the House of Commons rather than from some of his officials concerning these taxation measures.
I had occasion to remark the other day, although this may not be agreed with by some people, that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni had made the best speech, in my opinion, so far as veterans affairs are concerned; I still think the hon. member from Comox-Alberni has made the best speech in connection with this bill, and he made it tonight with respect to the amendment.
I enjoy listening to the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, when I can hear him, and I appreciate his knowledge of subjects such as this. Unfortunately, however, he still thinks he is speaking to a little board in one of those vested-interests small committee rooms on Bay street, Toronto, because we cannot hear what he says.
I do not think the government is right in its taxation of frigidaires, nor do I think it is right in its idea of taxing lower priced automobiles. I have not had the privilege of owning a Cadillac, like some of my lumber friends. I think the government is wrong in its taxation of lower priced automobiles and it is particularly wrong in taxing such things as electric irons. The minister cannot justify to me the taxation of an electric iron, which is a necessity to the veteran's wife in this modern day and age. He cannot justify to me the taxation of kerosene or gasoline frigidaires for the use of the farmer's wife, living many miles away from electrical power.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no taxation on kerosene refrigerators.

Unfortunately some of us in the far districts cannot always pick and choose. We must take what we can get. I suggest that if the minister had consulted some of the members of the House of Commons instead of some of the so-called advisers here he would not have committed the error in this respect.

Excise Tax Act Amendment
I want to explain my vote in this connection. I believe that this so-called austerity program is in the best interests of the people of Canada as a whole. Whether we like it or not, we are in this position with regard1 to our foreign exchange. I am not as optimistic as are some lion, members from Ontario with regard to future prospects for gold. I believe this is the best program we could develop. Therefore I intend to support the government and I shall oppose the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who would always move an amendment about anything, even the weather. I am quite prepared to go before the people of my riding and justify my stand. I disagree with the policy of my friend, the hon. member for one of the suburbs of Winnipeg. I disagree with the policy of the minister and of the government in connection with frigidaires, particularly country frigidaires; I disagree with their policy with regard to low-priced cars; I disagree with their policy with regard to electric irons. But I have yet to hear from the other side of the house one suggestion as to how we could better meet the emergency situation in which we find ourselves at the present time. While I believe that the minister's policy has its faults and1 its mistakes, I believe it is the best policy we have with which to meet the situation.

This afternoon when the hon. member for Temiscouata was criticizing the government for the policy involved in this particular measure, he made some reference to consistency and logic with particular reference to myself. I rather resented1 his remarks with respect to me, because I have always prided myself on being consistent and logical in what I say. If the hon. gentleman has any criticism to make of anything I have said in the past on economics or on the British North America Act, I suggest that he take the text of my remarks and indicate in what respect I have been inconsistent and illogical. I believe that the shoe is on the other foot. I think the hon. gentleman is the one who is illogical and inconsistent. On the one hand, he criticizes his party and the government for taxation policy and, on the other hand he does not suggest any alternative. Yet he has the audacity and the effrontery to ridicule and scoff at suggestions which emanate from this group. Furthermore, he indicates his inconsistency most definitely by voting opposite to the way in which he talks, when it comes to a vote. So, when it comes to a matter of consistency, I suggest that the hon. gentleman resort to a little introspection.
I think the only members of this house who have spoken logically on the principle involved in this particular bill and similar bills are the members of the Social Credit group. We have heard much criticism on the part of certain hon. gentlemen in the Liberal party; we have also heard a great deal of it from the Conservatives and from the C.C.F. But if they were in the seats of the mighty, what policy would they pursue? What would be their source of funds? What would be their method of attempting to achieve the results which the government alleges it is attempting to achieve? With regard to the Conservative party, I cannot imagine their using any different policies whatsoever from those which the government is using. They have not indicated that they have any other policy. If they are to reduce taxation in some respects, they must raise money by other means. Thus far they have not subscribed to the Social Credit way of doing it, and they have not any of their own. So I think they are certainly guilty of inconsistency as well.
I think the same reasoning can be applied to our C.C.F. friends. They moved an amendment this afternoon in an attempt to abolish at least one section of this measure, in order to reduce taxes which are being levied or which might be levied. But on the other hand, if they were in office and were managing the government, what would they use as a source of funds? How would they derive their revenue? So far as I am able to observe from listening to their statements, they would resort to taxation. They have not suggested any alternative. So whether, under their administration, they raise the money through this particular means or not, they would still have to resort to taxation. In advocating the policies which they have advocated, I cannot see how they can consider themselves to be consistent.
Therefore that leaves only the members of the Social Credit group who, in my opinion, have spoken consistently on this. All through the years we have advocated drastic reductions of taxation, even to the point of total elimination of dominion taxation. But we have not left it there. We have indicated an alternative for the raising of money.
What is your alternative?
I think the hon. gentleman knows it just as well as any of us who have made any remarks on the subject.
I should like to hear it again.

If the hon. member really wants to know, I will suggest to him that the
Excise Tax Act Amendment

government, which has the supreme prerogative over money, is not obliged to raise any money by taxation. It has at its disposal the power to create and issue all the money it needs.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.

All right, Mr. Chairman. I do not intend to launch into a discussion of money theories. I was just answering a question which the hon. gentleman put to me. But I repeat that I and my associates in the Social Credit group are definitely opposed to this measure. We stand for a drastic reduction of taxation, and we have indicated an alternative.
There is one aspect of the present situation which I think has not received the attention it should have received, namely, the positive side rather than the negative. The minister, his supporters and others have suggested that the objective of this measure is to curtail consumption. Why place so much emphasis on the curtailing of consumption? Why not look at it positively and consider whether we cannot do something more about stimulating production? That is an aspect which, according to my observation, has not received much emphasis during the course of this debate. I feel certain that one means of stimulating much production in this country is to reduce taxation. I am sure that every hon. member has heard farmers, workers and businessmen in general say that they would be glad to produce a little more but for taxation. What do we invariably hear? The farmer says, "Why should I raise my production when, as a consequence, I do nothing but pay more taxes?" The worker says the same thing, namely, "Why should I work overtime, bring my income up into the next bracket and penalize myself by so doing?" All the way through the whole economy we find that, as a result of taxation, there is a certain amount of discouragement of production.
Therefore I suggest that we place a little more emphasis on the positive side of our program and see whether we cannot do something by way of stimulating production, and thus provide ourselves with more goods with which to take care of the needs abroad and of ourselves. I think the best way to do that would be to remove those elements of our economic life which discourage production, one of which, in my opinion, is taxation. So I suggest that the policy involved in this resolution can do nothing but discourage still further the production of very much needed goods in this country. Therefore I, together with my

associates, will oppose it; and I personally think the whole thing should be consigned to the nether regions.

I have a question to ask, Mr. Chairman, but I did not know whether I should put it in another form. We have been discussing this matter since before Christmas, and there has been a great deal of repetition. Even today the minister said more than once, "Again I say"; "I repeat", and so on. I know in the British house there is a way of dealing with this situation; and I am going to ask you, Mr. Chairman, if we have anything in our parliamentary laws or our procedure which will permit us to close off this debate and get on with other business.
Mr. Chairman-
I think I should have an answer to my question.

One reason my hon. friend does not get an answer to his question is that under our rules he cannot question the Chair, and that seems to deal with that matter. I am going to take only three or four minutes, which I am sure will please my old friend the hon. member for Fort William.
Thank you.

My hon. friend was a much better soccer football player than parliamentarian. He never won a game playing football, so that will give the committee an idea of my estimate of his ability as a parliamentarian.
I am opposed to this resolution, Mr. Chairman, and I want to tell you why. When I listened to the minister on the evening of November 17 I could understand a good many things he said; but when he came to the matter of this excise tax I got lost. I have studied everything he has said since then and everything anyone else has said in connection with this proposal, and this idea struck me. I think it is elementary that if this excise tax merely raises the price of Canadian goods, that is inflation. If it fails and purchases do not continue, that means unemployment. I submit, sir, that today I am in exactly the same position. This thing can go in one of two ways, the one toward inflation and the other toward unemployment. Those of us who live in or have knowledge of the smaller places in Canada know the small businesses which have been wrecked by this measure, and in such cases it has meant unemployment.

Excise Tax Act Amendment
I confess that in listening to the minister I heard two things with which I would be in agreement. One was that we could save United States exchange by an embargo on United States goods. The other was that to the extent we could supplant United States goods by the increased manufacture of similar goods in Canada, to that extent also we would save United States exchange. But if this tax means that we are to decrease that manufacture, then it goes straight against one of the things which the minister spoke of and which he had in mind at that time.
The other evening I asked the minister a few questions. I intend to paraphrase them this evening, if I may. I hope I may do so correctljq but if I fail in that I hope I may be immediately interrupted. The minister said he did not know now, after four months of the operation of the tax, whether or not it was in fact saving United States exchange. Then I asked when he would know, and he went farther and said he was in doubt that he would ever know, because his scheme was three-pronged and he was unable to separate the prongs. As you know, Mr. Chairman, there is a very well known instrument used on a farm, an instrument which is also threepronged. The minister does not know whether he has a sheaf of oats on one prong and perhaps some rather less valuable product on the other. His whole attitude was that he could not tell whether or not this measure was in fact helping the scheme for saving United States dollars.
Therefore, sir-and I close with this-I take the position that I was right in my impression when I listened to the minister on November 17, that internally it meant inflation in one way, if people bought the goods, but that in the other direction it meant unemployment if it raised prices so high that people could not buy them. I still abide by that view; and now, having come here and heard the minister tell me he did not know whether or not this was helping to save United States exchange and that he did not think he ever would know, speaking for the people of this country who are paying these inflated prices, or who cannot buy because they are unable to pay the prices, I am opposed to this measure and will so vote.

speechtext:

out of order. At that time you quoted citation 500 from Beauchesne, third edition; and, incidentally, that is the same paragraph which the Minister of Finance and I were quoting from May, thirteenth edition, at pages 543 and 544. The sentence you emphasized was the following:
Amendments, therefore, can be proposed to substitute another tax, of equivalent amount, for that proposed by the government, as, for instance, a proposal to substitute probate and legacy duty on real property as an alternative for an inhabited house duty, the necessity of new taxation, to that extent, being already declared on behalf of the crown.

In the original resolution there was included a tax on electric or gas refrigerators and also a tax on electric stoves. I should like to ask the minister why he relaxed the tax on electric stoves on December 8. There must have been some basic reason why the tax was taken off electric stoves. The fact of the matter is that the people who buy electric stoves are the people who buy electric refrigerators. To my mind there is discrimination in favour of one industry and against another when you leave a tax on one article and take it off the other. That is one incongruity.
The second incongruity seems to be in connection with one of the answers the minister gave me this afternoon in which he said that the tax was put on, as I understood him, so as not to permit production to rise in the Dominion of Canada upon goods with United States content, produced for export, beyond the confines of Canada. If it is the purpose of the resolution to block in a sense the production of too large an amount of goods in the country, that seems to be completely at variance with the remarks of the minister of external affairs at Winnipeg on January 23 last when he said that the purpose of the government was to create a genuine exportable surplus large enough to enable us to play our part in the recovery of Europe without having to resort to crippling import restrictions. To my mind the exposition of the matter given by the minister of external affairs and the exposition of this resolution given by the Minister of Finance do not jibe.
There is one other matter I wanted to bring to the minister's attention. The minister said on March 18, as reported on page 2373 of Hansard:
I have hail numerous discussions with representative groups of car manufacturers, and radio manufacturers, because they are two of the larger groups. The car manufacturers do not claim that the tax has yet slowed down the consumption of cars. They tell me that they think it will. Whether they are right or wrong, I do not know. The same thing applies to the radio people. No one has contended to me that the sale of radios has yet been diminished.
I am sure all hon. members have received a memorandum from the radio manufacturers' association of Canada under date of March 5 last. I presume the minister has already read this release, but I should like to call his attention to section 6 on page 3 where it says:
In November, 1947, the last month prior to the effect of the new 25 per cent excise tax, the member companies of our association produced 103,000 radio receivers (not including export production) and reported sales for the same month totalling 102,000 radios. Substantial sales drops were noted in December and in January, 1948, the same companies sold only 39.000 radio receivers-a 62 per cent drop from November. This also represents a drop of over 40 per cent from the sales by the same companies in January of 1947.
Final figures for February sales and production are not yet available but indications are that still further drops have occurred and already there have been drastic cutbacks in factory production and employment.
I should like hon. members to note those last few words, "drastic cutbacks in factory production and employment." We shall have a vote on this matter pretty soon. The minister said a short time ago that he did not know of any drop in sales of radios, but here are figures given by responsible people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am delighted to hear that the tax is doing what it was intended to do, but I do not believe that that is possible.

There was a drastic drop of 62 per cent from November. I want ta ask the minister whether the intention of this tax is to put the radio industry out of business or whether he ought not to regulate, first and foremost, a situation which could be alleviated in quite a different way from the manner in which he is doing it. I should like to quote a clipping from the Wall Street Journal, as follows:
The more one thinks of it the proposals to deflate buying and stop prices going up by increasing taxation are very dangerous ones. If the government increases taxation, it will spend the money it gets. It inflates its own costs with the avowed object of deflating others.
That is the very thing we are doing with this resolution. The minister must know by now that this is the most unpopular tax that has been before this house in a long time. It is not only unpopular in the house; it is unpopular in the country. I think, as a matter of fact, he is going to stifle the exportation of those products which we have been trying to build up production on, for a long while in this country. If he does not know it, then somebody should tell him right now, while we are dealing with this matter, that there has been a sloughing off of production and a sloughing off of buying in this country. In my opinion this will be considered one of the worst taxes we have had for a long time.

I am reluctant to rise at. this late stage, but I feel I would be remiss in my duty if I did not say a few words at this time. While I believe the measure itself has every indication of proving its value, there' are some things in it with which I do not agree. I always believe that you can catch more flies with honey than you can with salt or pepper.

I want to make a personal appeal to the minister tonight with regard to refrigerators. If the minister would say to the committee that refrigerators were being taken off the list everyone in the house would let this bill go through.
A refrigerator is essential in the modern home. I know the minister has one and I know all the men who drew up the bill have refrigerators. Wherever electric power has been developed throughout the country, wherever it has been put through rural constituencies, wherever power is available, the people want refrigerators. They have been saving their money for a long time, expecting that their chance would come to get a refrigerator. They now find this tax imposed, which will make them pay $100 more for a refrigerator. That will not stop them from getting one because it is a necessity, but it is a mean tax and the people resent it terribly. A refrigerator, by keeping meat, butter, eggs and other provisions fresh, enables people to cut their living costs by ten per cent. Tonight I picked up a menu in the Chateau Laurier, a Canadian National hotel, and I found printed on it a notice "Excise tax 25 per cent."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You must have been in the grill.
Dancing.

want to know by what authority meals are being taxed?

I should like to make one last appeal to the Minister of Finance. Unfortunately we on this side of the house cannot make personal appeals to the minister, so I shall not attempt that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why not? Some people do. I have mo restrictions on personal appeals.

This is a resolution which
affects the public as a whole and is not the personal hobby of the Minister of Finance. It was introduced on behalf of the government, and so any appeals made in the house with respect to it should be made to the house.

What kind of car do you drive?

speechtext: Order. Excess profits are beyond the scope of this resolution.
If that is your ruling, Mr. Chairman, I am very happy to bow to it.

I have two or three questions to ask the minister. An embargo has been put on certain United States products. A certain amount of customs duties was collected on these products in the year before the embargo was imposed. Can the minister tell the committee what amount of duty was collected on all these items now forbidden entry to Canada, during the year before the imposition of the embargo?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That question came up under Bill No. 3, and I gave some information then as to importations in the previous year of the articles which are prohibited. I have not that information here on this bill, because this tax does not apply to those goods.

I understand that, since the government is being deprived of a certain amount of customs revenue on United States products which can no longer enter Canada, a 25 per cent excise tax was imposed on Canadian products as compensation for that loss of customs duty on United States goods.

speechtext: That was not the intention in putting it on. It was, as I have said, to deter the consumption of goods for a variety of reasons which have been discussed here a number of times. This is my last word. I do not very well understand the imposition of this tax, but I will warn the minister again, and I
will tell him that, while I am not opposed to all the officials of his department, I am opposed to some of them. I have not much support in the house when I complain in this regard, but it will be necessary before the next Liberal convention to have a spring cleaning among the top ranking officials of the Department of Finance, and I say that in all friendliness to the minister and to everyone in the government.
