Exactly what is the situation now in regard to kerosene refrigerators? Were they taken off this list where the excise tax is and put in one of the other schedules?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They were never included.
We can still get kerosene refrigerators?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know whether kerosene refrigerators are made in this country. I do not think they are, although it is possible that some manufacturers may be able to produce them. I do not think they are made here. At present, importation is prohibited, but I have promised to give consideration to the setting up of a quota for that type of refrigerator under the other bill, Bill No. 3, because such a refrigerator is used primarily in rural areas where other refrigerators are not available.

The case of kerosene refrigerators is very much the same as the case of motorcars. When one looks at the situation in regard to motorcars, one wonders that the government do not take a different attitude, particularly in view of all that they have said in connection wdth this proposed legislation. For a while, motorcars were like kerosene refrigerators, banned completely; but since November last the minister has finally arrived at a quota for motorcars. As I understand it, and if I do not have it correctly I hope the minister will let me know, there is a certain amount of United States exchange allowed to be used for the importation of motorcars. Am I right in that, that a certain amount of United States exchange is allowed for the importation of motorcars and parts?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

Now that the government has settled the amount of United States exchange which shall be allotted for imported motorcars or parts, why does it still insist upon putting an excise tax on motorcars, ranging in the lower priced vehicles from 25 per cent to 75 per cent in the higher? The
Excise Tax Act Amendment

minister has said that the purpose of the legislation is not to gather revenue for the crown, because it has already more revenue than it knows what to do with. The purpose is to save exchange. But here we have the government allocating exactly and precisely how much United States exchange shall be allowed for the importation of motorcars, so that whether people want to buy far more than would otherwise be available, they cannot in Canada because there is only so much United States exchange.
I have not heard explained to the committee just why the government still insists on using the excise tax, because it seems to me it has already made a restriction, when it saw fit, by allowing just so many United States dollars to be used for the importation of United States motorcars and parts. The result of the present regulations is that those who have the longest purses will be able to get motorcars, while those who cannot afford to pay these extraordinary taxes, the money not being needed by the government, will have to do without any kind of vehicle.
It does seem indeed that such a form of legislation, such a spirit behind legislation, is entirely wrong, because there are still many people who were overseas, who did not have a chance to get a motorcar, and now that they are finding their place in the business world, they would like to enjoy some of the facilities which the average Canadian citizen enjoys, but they find they are up against a 25 per cent tax as a minimum. I can see no reason for it and, as far as I know, the government has not advanced any satisfactory reason, because it has said that there is only so much exchange for the purpose of bringing in motorcars, and when that is exhausted you cannot bring in any more.
We find, therefore, that there will be a certain amount of unemployment created, even in the subsidiary motorcar industries, and that brings me to the larger field of these excise taxes and their effect on employment. There is hardly a towm, hardly a hamlet in this country that has not suffered by reason of the excise taxes which the government has put on, and the sad part about these excise taxes, and the unemployment they create, is that in the great majority of cases the firms involved were new firms made up of veterans. These young men cannot now obtain the substance of their business, so that they have to close up; or if they take the word of the Minister of Trade and Commerce they may look upon these restrictions as of a temporary nature until such time as the government is able to bring its United States exchange

account into better balance, and they may go to their banks and endeavour to get enough working capital to keep their shows going, hoping that each passing month may see the end of their troubles. As a matter of fact, those of us who are here and who have looked at the problem realize that the time is most indefinite, and when the minister mentions months he may have meant years. So that these young men who have started up business might as well have folded up and let their staffs go.
In one case a group of veterans from the navy and the air force had already 115 people employed. They were importing radios and other household electrical machines from the United States, and they found they were absolutely without any further source of supply when these bans became effective last November. They have had to go out of business, throwing out of employment nearly 100 people. Some are keeping on in the hope that they will eventually, in not too long a time, be able to start up in business again.
Inj the same city I am thinking of, another company that is severely affected by the ban on the importation of fresh vegetables and fruits had to let 250 people go because there is no volume now to be handled; when the summer crops of our own vegetables and fruits come in there will not be the men to handle the produce, and the cost of merchandising will go up substantially. All of these are strong reasons against the passing of these resolutions. As a matter of fact when one considers the taxes on motorcars alone, it must be realized that even on the cheapest four-door sedan car the excise tax is $268.05, and the sales tax on top of that is S85.78, or a total tax-without even the duty or any of the various other things included-on the cheapest four-door car in the country of no less than $353.83. To my mind that is a shocking burden to put upon the young man, particularly the veteran, who wants to get a new car. Most of the population were perhaps fairly well supplied before and, like the minister himself, may have the pleasure of driving a 1939 model, as I think he mentioned to the house the other night.
I feel that these excise taxes were put on for no other reason than to satisfy the feelings or the prospective feelings. I might even have called them, of the United States administration. We were careful, because of our requirements of vital products of the United States, not to offend them in any possible way. We have put on these heavy excise taxes and have caused unemployment and an increase in the cost of living in our own country. As a matter of fact, it would

Excise Tax Act Amendment
be interesting to know, and I think before we close this debate, we should hear from the Minister of Finance in this regard, just what progress he is making with the United States government in regard to tariff regulations. I understand that, since we put on these excise taxes, the United States administration, when it comes to the payment of customs tariff, assess their customs rate against the Canadian price plus the excise taxes in Canada. This, of course, makes it prohibitive for the Canadian manufacturer to export to United States markets. We have already found that there has been a certain amount of tinkering or changing of the schedules, because the minister realizes that we just cannot put out of business many manufacturing concerns in Canada who would be able to export to the United States were it not for the fact that we have these excise taxes on here, and that United States officials, for tariff purposes, assess their duty against the Canadian price plus our excise tax.
We have seen what the administration here have done when they run into circumstances like that. They have withdrawn certain articles like golf clubs-and I think the minister mentioned one or two others the other evening-from the list of articles which would be subject to the excise tax. I think we should know about this. We have always looked upon our neighbours to the south as friendly and co-operative, and we hope that they are living in the spirit of Geneva just as we in this country are not only living in that spirit but are going farther and are extremely careful not to do anything to offend our neighbours to the south. I think we should have a clearance from that country, so that what little export we were doing in certain lines would not be completely obliterated because we now have a domestic excise tax. The minister should give some indication as to what progress has been made in Washington in that regard before we are asked to make any decision on this vital matter.
It has always been of great concern to me that neither the Minister of Finance nor the Minister of Trade and Commerce, so far as this committee has learned, has made any strenuous effort to increase the export of Canadian products to the United States. Certainly one would have felt that last June or July, when they saw the situation getting so desperate with regard to United States exchange, before they contemplated measures such as we have before us today they would have thought of alternative measures, and in particular would have endeavoured-both of them, I should have thought-to go to the
United States to see if the United States government would not make it possible for that country to use about one-half of one per cent of its total national income for increased imports from this country. Then our whole problem of United States exchange would have disappeared. But we have had no indication whatsoever in regard to that.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.
Quite so. I think I am in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member should deal with the resolution.

I have the resolution before me. The resolution is that the excise tax be placed on certain articles set out in the schedule. The whole purpose of that resolution is in order to raise United States exchange or to prevent the use of United States exchange by Canadians. So I am suggesting that both ministers, in place of going to the United States just to borrow some money and to humiliate our country, might have done something in order to see if the people of the United States would not have taken more Canadian products; because, while they talk about full employment-and I think that is an expression they have used in this debate on a number of occasions-full employment is not necessarily the same as full production. If one has working everybody who could reasonably be expected, to work, it is still possible to get more modern machinery. That is one of the things the manufacturers and industrialists of this country have been doing in the last two or three years. When we get more modern machines, we can turn out more goods and men are released to do other things. There are plenty of opportunities for them in a great variety of fields as the present time. Therefore I feel that the government have not handled this question in a way which was constructive but, on the other hand, have endeavoured to put Canadians out of employment. It made little difference to the government on whom they put these taxes, as long as they were not affected themselves. But if it were their ox that was gored, they would soon realize what the feeling is across the country from one end to the other. There is not a town or hamlet in which there is not a number of firms, particularly younger firms, which have not been disastrously affected by the excise taxes which are now before this committee.

I should like to ask the Minister of Finance one question in connection with automobiles.
Excise Tax Act Amendment

Mr. MoIVOR: Just one question?

Yes. In the Financial Post an article appeared recently which stated that one British automobile manufacturer could supply the total quota that Great Britain was allowed for manufactured cars. Since several British plants have been re-tooled to produce cars which would meet Canadian conditions better than they have in the past, will the minister consider increasing the British quota?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is under the other measure. That is under Bill No. 3, which we have already passed. I am not familiar with the quota situation with regard to British cars, but that comes under import restrictions which are imposed under the measure the house has already passed.

At this stage of the debate it would be presumptuous on my part to do anything that might appear to sound like offering advice to the minister. I know it would be rejected. But even at this stage I wish to offer the minister what seem to me sound reasons why, particularly in the light of things that have happened today and things that have been said this evening, he should withdraw this measure. The minister smiles. I want to assure him that in what I have to say tonight I am going to deal seriously with points he has raised in this debate, because I think they ought to be seriously answered. I am going to direct my remarks this evening, and they will be brief, to the minister in the hope that he will listen to reason even at this stage; that he will forget about matters of saving face and sit down deliberately and think about this measure in the light of statements that have come from his own side of the house tonight.
It is quite apparent that if hon. members on the other side were free to speak their minds on this matter it would arouse on the government side of the house such a tide of opposition to this measure that the minister would be compelled to withdraw it or face defeat upon it.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: How do you know that?

In answer to my hon. friend the Postmaster General, I think enough members on the other side of the house have spoken tonight on this measure in rebellious terms to make it quite clear that they do not stand alone on this matter, that they are simply the more courageous of those who entertain rebellious feelings concerning this measure. Theirs are not simply voices crying

in the wilderness, from the other side of the chamber. I for one am convinced, Mr. Chairman, that they do speak for many of the members sitting to your right in this chamber.
Speak for yourself.

I will speak for myself, and I will also speak my mind concerning the remarks of some who have spoken tonight. Surely this afternoon the minister had proof abundant of the utter unpopularity of this measure with his own supporters in this house; and he certainly has abundant proof of the unpopularity-yes,	the	unacceptability-of
this measure throughout the country.
I said I would deal seriously with some points the minister has advanced in support of his measure. I do not propose to repeat what I said in this house, recently on the constitutional aspects. At the conclusion of those remarks a week or so ago I was challenged by the hon. member for Halton, who in effect said that because I had confined myself to the constitutional, or rather the unconstitutional, aspects,of the measure, therefore apparently I did not have any other objections to it. I assure you, Mr. Chairman, that I have an abundance of objections to this measure, any one of which, if placed before people who are free to express their minds, would be sufficient to condemn the measure.
First, what are the grounds on which the minister relies to justify an unconstitutional measure which seeks to increase the load under which the round-shouldered taxpayers of this country are groaning today? In the first place he says it will help the United States dollar situation. In the course of this debate the minister has had an abundance of opportunity to prove to this committee where and how any saving of United States dollars will be made, and he has utterly and completely failed to do so. It is not without significance that the minister had not one figure to bring before the committee as to the estimated saving of United States dollars. If, as the minister professed it to be, that was a principal objective of this measure, then certainly common sense and even the most elementary requirements of this House of Commons would have dictated that he must have some estimate of the saving in United States dollars to put before the committee in justification of this sweeping measure. We have debated this matter; we have asked questions and repeated them, and we still have to hear from the minister one word concerning the estimated saving of United States dollars. Think of it. Here we are, four months and more since the minister made his radio announcement on

Excise Tax Act Amendment
November 17; and even at this late date he has no estimate of the saving of United States dollars this measure is said to be capable of bringing about. When will he get it? If ever there was a fine example of blundering on the part of a government, it is this. The minister says it will save United States dollars. Four months later he has not even an estimate of the quantity of United States dollars that will be saved. Can one imagine any more complete condemnation of this measure than that fact alone? Not one item of proof is brought before us that this will save a single United States dollar; but as a parliament we are asked to penalize the Canadian consumer and the Canadian producer, to take a jump in the dark because the Minister of Finance, without the slightest element of proof, says that somehow this measure will save United States dollars. If this House of Commons has not taken leave of its senses it will not heap these penalties upon the Canadian consumer and the Canadian producer, without some proof of benefit with respect to the saving of United States dollars beyond what we have heard so far.
So much for that argument. The next point advanced by the minister in his speech in this house on December 16, as reported at page 336 of Hansard, in effect was this: We do not want to do any harm to United States producers ; we want to preserve a market for them here in Canada. These were his words:
But by imposing these excise taxes we are doing something to protect the legitimate longer-range interests of these businesses.
What are these businesses? These are the United States producers and their dealer organizations here. He went on:
While the Canadian manufacturers are temporarily relieved of competition from the United States, their unexpected advantage is being at least partly offset by the effects of the special taxes. Without these taxes, prices of many of the articles affected could have risen a good deal, to the benefit of the manufacturers and distributors.
As a result of the taxes, it is the public treasury that benefits.
To me that is the most transparent exposure of the iniquity of this measure. The minister seeks to justify it on the ground that, while he is denjdng the Canadian consumer the things that consumer wants and has had hitherto, he will not permit the Canadian producer to step into the breach and fill the requirements of the Canadian consumer. "No", he says; "we will keep the Canadian producer out of the field. Why? Well, we do not want to hurt the United States producer. Therefore we will keep both
the Canadian and the United States producer out of this field. The Canadian consumer can do without, or he can submit to the penalty of an additional 25 per cent impost. But we will give no benefit to the Canadian producer; we will treat the Canadian producer and the United States producer on a footing of equality in this respect." That is proof enough to me, Mr. Chairman, that this measure is worthy only of the condemnation of this house.
Then, as a third argument, and a sort of merry-go-round argument it is, the minister says: "Oh, we will use this fiscal method. We will drain off purchasing power by this added tax. We will slow down consumption." Let us analyse that argument. I call it an audacious argument. If that argument is sound in this particular, then surely it is sound in other particulars as well. So the minister is putting before the committee the argument that it is good government policy in times like these to soak the taxpayer, to make him pay money to the federal treasury so that he will not have money left to spend on the goods he needs. If that is a sound argument as applied to goods within the range enumerated in this resolution, then if this committee chooses to give its imprimatur to that argument we may be very sure the minister will take fresh courage and be prepared to apply this argument to other goods as well. Where do you stop with an argument like that? I say to the minister that measures of this kind, applied to a range of goods which include many downright necessities, are inflationary. The minister has not confined himself, in the enumeration before us, to those articles which are clearly of the luxury class. Far from it. Just look at some of them, and then let any hon. member say that these are not necessities for many Canadians.
Think of them! Irons! The minister says that the Canadian housewife can do without electric irons because, they are not a necessity. "Go and heat your iron on a woodstove"- apparently that is the argument of the minister. He says to the Canadian housewife, "You do not need an electric iron. An electric iron is not a necessity for you."
Then, who will say that razors are not a necessity? Is the minister proclaiming a new fashion in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Electric razors are not a necessity.

I should have thought electric razors were a necessity for some people.
Excise Tax Act Amendment

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have never used one, myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: The hon. member does not need a razor.

I cannoit hear some of the remarks from hon. members over there. Let the minister rise in his place and say that electric toasters are not a necessity in Canada. How many Canadian housewives in areas where there is any electric current available are prepared to agree with the minister when he says that electric toasters are luxuries the housewife can do without? Let the minister stand up on a public platform in Canada and tell the housewives of Canada that electric toasters are luxuries they must do without. Let him have the courage to tell them that. He is saying to the Canadian housewife, "Just you buy an electric toaster, and I will levy a 25 per cent tax against you." And when that is done he tells us it is done in the name of draining off surplus purchasing power! Whose purchasing power is he draining off? Is it the purchasing power of -the wealthy? No, it is not the wealthy who are suffering from this fax. If we have had any discriminatory measures before this House of Commons at the present session-and we certainly have had a number of them-this piece of legislation is the most discriminatory of them all. It is the rankest kind of discrimination against the people of small means.
Does the minister mean -to tell me that the housewife who wishes to have a cheap electric toaster-not an expensive automatic toaster, but just a cheap electric toaster-is to be called upon by this government to -pay a 25 per cent impost upon it. And he tells this to us in the name of directing the Canadian economy along paths which are in keeping with the government plan.
If the government is prepared to admit that it is embarking upon an era of planned economy, then here is apparently the first long step in the process. For my part, I do not want any of this government's planning of the affairs of the people of Canada, when the minister conceives it to be government policy, and a necessity on the part of the government, to say to the housewife who is already having a hard enough time to make ends meet, "If you want to buy a new toaster, even a cheap one to replace your broken toaster, I am going to charge you an additional 25 per cent tax on it, because I think it is good for you and also for the Canadian economy."

That is what the minister is saying to the housewife today. He says he knows better than the housewife how her dollar ought to be spent. And he says this is -not an inflationary measure. What is it that causes inflation? Surely it is a situation wherein the supply of goods is -not adequate to fake up the purchasing power. How is the minister to justify this -tax as an anti-inflationary measure? He puts -these things beyond the reach of people who -need them, people of small means.
These taxes are not eonfi-ned to expensive articles. These are taxes which are applied to all articles of the kind, regardless of how dear or how cheap they may be. And to me, that is a complete exposure of the fallacy of the minister's argument in support of what he calls his fiscal policy.
The last argument the minister has dared to advance in- support of this iniquitous measure is that the government can very well do with the revenue. Is it not amazing talk coming from this government which, for many months past, has been busy cheering itself and shouting from the housetops about the great surplus it has been rolling up this year? How did this surplus come about? Well, we shall have something to say about that at the -proper time, as to whether it is a genuine surplus or not. But let us take it on the basis upon which the government has put it forward. It is boasting about having a surplus of three-quarters of a billion dollars in the first eight or nine months of the fiscal year. The minister says, in the face of that,. "We can do with the revenue from this measure".

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I suggest that the hon. member confine his remarks. to this measure.

I say most emphatically
I am dealing with this measure. I am answering the argument -put forward by the Minister-of Finance in support of this very measure, when he said he could very well do with the revenue from it. We will- find his words at. page-

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I would suggest that the hon. member speak louder and address the Chair.

Mr. Chairman, I will speak as loudly as it is necessary in order to be heard in this chamber. I shall continue to address you, sir, and I suggest to the minister who has just spoken that for once he make a serious endeavour to abide by the rules of the house which call upon a member to rise

Excise Tax Act Amendment
in his place and ask permission to ask a question, and not to blurt out these interpolations as he is doing. It has got to'the point where no one takes his observations in the middle of a speech seriously any more.
Here is what the minister said. At page 336 of Hansard, dealing with this measure, along with other measures, he said, "At the same time, additional revenue will not be unwelcome." At a time like this, when the rank and file of the Canadian people are having a difficult time to meet the rising costs of living, and when they are having a difficult time to meet their tax burden, and at a time when the minister has been boasting from the housetops about his unprecedented budget surplus, how has he the temerity, I say, to come before the House of Commons of Canada to seek to justify an additional impost upon the ground that he can do with the additional revenue that it promises? Any minister of finance at a time like this who seriously puts before the House of Commons that argument, in purported justification of a demand for an additional impost upon the Canadian people, has forfeited any right to be taken seriously in the House of Commons in what he says.
Indirect taxes, again! We on this side of the house have been fighting against this crushing load of indirect taxes. This is the kind of tax which bears so heavily upon the consumer. This is the kind of tax which bears relatively so much more heavily upon the man of small means than upon the man of larger means. We fought that fight last year. We are going on fighting that battle over again for the small man in this country, against the attempt by this government to heap the load upon him. The small man may not see these hidden taxes which bear so heavily upon him. Here we have a government which has already this year taken out of the pockets of the Canadian people more than a billion dollars in indirect taxation. They like to do it, because they think the Canadian taxpayer does not realize how much he is paying in these hidden taxes. The money is coming out of their pockets just the same; and the Minister of Finance thinks that somehow these taxes will be so hidden in the price of the commodities the consumer has to buy that he will not notice the tax, and that he will not have any way of voicing his true opinion and his resentment against these additional levies.
The government policy, if you can say that this government has a policy at all, is just so shot through with contradiction that it is utterly impossible to rationalize what the
government is doing. It is talking in one breath about the cost of living; we are hearing a great deal about how important it is that people should keep down prices, but here this government, by the most deliberate and barefaced act, is seeking to increase those prices, not by five per cent or ten per cent but by 25 per cent. It is a shocking demonstration of duplicity on the part of the government, a contradiction in every term. The government is contradicting itself. In one breath the government is talking about the desirability of keeping down the cost of living, and then the government turns around and, by its next act, adds to the cost of living with these iniquitous and exorbitant imposts.
We have been hearing something about inventory profits, profits that come about by reason of the advances in prices. Just a few days ago the Minister of Finance told this house in committee that he was aware that inventory profits had been taken by retailers on goods on their shelves which were within the classes enumerated in this resolution, even though the tax had not been paid upon them. Let this be known to the Canadian people throughout the length and breadth of Canada! He said he would not blame them for doing so. He said he would not blame the retailer for advancing the prices of articles on his shelves in these classes of goods by the 25 per cent, even though they had not paid the tax. He said he would not blame them, that it was all right to take an inventory mark-up in that way.
Do you realize, Mr. Chairman, what that means? The dominion Minister of Finance is saying to the Canadian retailer, "All right; go ahead; charge up your 25 per cent on the cost of these articles as you sell them over the counter to the consumer. It is all right; you have not paid the tax on them, but we are taxing some fellow farther back and by and by, some months from now, you may be getting some of these tax-paid goods on your shelves; but it is all right; put on your mark-up now." That is the very government which has been deprecating mark-ups by retailers in other respects, but approves them as long as they are related to this government's iniquitous tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has been standard practice ever since confederation.

The minister says it has been standard practice. I say to him that is the old story. Every time I pick up Hansard following my having said anything I find Hansard larded up with the interjections of the minister.
Excise Tax Act Amendment

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the first interjection I have made in thirty minutes.

He puts his interjections on Hansard in contravention to the rules of the house. When I pick up Hansard the next day I find his quips on Hansard. He should either follow the rules of the house or just let us have a free-for-all discussion without regard to the rules of the house. It is just not fair for some to be compelled to follow the rules of the house, while the Minister of Finance regards himself as standing above all the rules of the house.
Let it be known that the Minister of Finance has condoned a 25 per cent mark-up on goods of the classes enumerated in this resolution as long as they were on the shelves of the retailer before the enactment of these taxes which were imposed by a radio announcement on November 17, whether the tax had been paid or not. The minister says it is standard practice. He knows it has been done. He was apparently aware that it would be done. He apparently approved it. I say to him that would cause any responsible minister to hesitate before imposing such an iniquitous tax, if he knew it would occasion inventory profits of 25 per cent.
Is the hon. member trying to talk this out? We would like to know whether he is trying to delay the legislation or not?
I know the hon. member and I think his question is quite unworthy of any hon. member in this house.
No.

I think he knows me well enough to know that I am perfectly serious in what I am doing. I shall certainly finish before eleven o'clock. If there are a few more interruptions I am quite prepared to answer them, but those who make the interruptions or cause them to be made must take full responsibility for the length of time consumed in making necessary answers.
You require no further proof of the utter irresponsibility of a measure of this kind, the utter iniquity of the imposition of a tax imposed over the radio than the fact that the minister has changed these most illegal taxes. Taxes have been removed from some of the original classes, just because the minister has waved his hand and said, "They are off." Then he says to the people, "You can get the taxes back." How are the people who paid these taxes or who paid the inventory mark-up to get them back? How many purchasers will be able to go back to the retailers and give proof of having paid this 25 per cent? It might be

all right in the case of a small store with a small clientele, but it would be quite impossible in the case-of large stores. People do not keep track of these things. They did not know that they would have an opportunity of going back and collecting this 25 per cent tax. They did not know that the minister would change his mind and see in part the folly of his ways. I wish he had seen it completely. The whole thing has just thrown Canadian business into a turmoil so far as the classes of goods enumerated in this resolution are concerned. This is my final word.
Oh, oh.
If hon. members opposite knew how they encourage me, perhaps they would not be quite so vociferous.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Only ten minutes more.

My final word to the Minister of Finance is this. He may feel that there is a question of personal prestige or face involved in his standing subbornly on this tax. I wish to assure him as one who, I think, is giving him better counsel than a lot of people around him, that he will be a bigger man in the eyes of the Canadian people if he comes forward now and admits his mistake and withdraws this tax. The minister knows that such withdrawal would be received with acclaim throughout the length and breadth of Canada.
If the minister persists stubbornly in the imposition of this tax, this tax which has been conceived in illegality, which has been levied illegally, which has been exacted at the expense of the constitution and extorted from the people of Canada, then I tell him that this government and the minister will be sorry for it one day. The best advice that anyone can give to the Minister of Finance today is that he forget about questions of personal prestige or political face and stand up courageously and manfully, and withdraw this resolution.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure that you will have noticed the great anxiety shown by my hon. friends on the other side of the house in the last few minutes to come to a vote. This afternoon they had an opportunity to be here to vote, and they did not show very much desire to be here and vote. Having regard to what occurred this afternoon, I do not think it is out of place at this time to discuss in general this resolution and to put to the minister some questions that still remain unanswered.
I have not taken part in this discussion, but one matter I did want to bring to the attention of the minister has to do in general with the excise tax. I refer particularly to the excise
tax on tobacco and, in particular, to tobacco that will be exported within the next few months to Europe and the continent under the Marshall plan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no reference to that in this resolution.

No, but I intend to ask that it be included. The situation today in so far as the tobacco industry is concerned is that in 1947 in this country 98,146 acres of tobacco were grown, with a total production of 90.360,000 pounds. On that tobacco there is, of course, a very great excise tax. I am not rising for the purpose of taking up any extra time but I want to bring this to the attention of the minister. I recently visited in that part of Ontario where the tobacco industry has advanced by leaps and bounds within the last few years. My understanding is that this year there is a possibility that there will be a production over and above what will be consumed in Canada or be exported. Having regard to the fact that, under the Marshall plan when it comes into existence, purchases will be made in Canada for export to Europe and that one of the things greatly desired in Europe is cigarettes, my suggestion with a view to increasing production in this country is that the minister should make provision whereby, in so far as exports of tobacco are concerned under the Marshall plan to Europe and generally to other parts of the world where the plan will be applied, the government of Canada remove the excise tax from such exports. That would give encouragement to the production of tobacco in this country.

Just before I leave the chair, may I recall that the hon. member for Fort William asked a question this afternoon in regard to the rules in the British house, and I think I should tell him what the rule is there.
